h1: Writing a project report for a gin distillery
title: A Project Report for a Gin Distillery | Craft Beer School
desc: What a detailed project report for a gin distillery should contain: scope, technical plan, costs, cash flow, licensing steps and a sensitivity check.
teaser: Banks and agencies often want a formal report, not a pitch. Here is what goes in it and how to keep it honest.
standfirst: A detailed project report, or DPR, is the formal case for a plant. It describes what you will build, what it costs and how it will be paid for. Lenders read it for gaps, so write it for a sceptic.
sections:
In India a detailed project report is the standard document that banks and some state agencies ask for when you seek a loan or support for a new unit. Elsewhere it may be called a feasibility study or an investment case. The structure is similar: scope, technical plan, costs, finance and risks.

The report is not the same as a business plan. A plan argues for the idea. A project report documents how it will be built and funded, with enough technical detail that an outsider can check it.

Describe the process from neutral spirit receipt to filled bottle. Include the still type and size, botanical handling, dilution water treatment, filtration, filling and storage. Give the batch size and the number of batches per week you plan to run. Add the utilities: power, water, steam or heating and effluent.

Layout matters because ethanol is flammable. Show how you will store spirit, ventilate the still room and meet fire and safety requirements. Say plainly that you will follow the standards of your jurisdiction and name who will check them.

Break capital into land or premises, building work, plant and machinery, installation, licences and approvals, pre-operative expenses and working capital. Use supplier quotations, not guesses. Say so in the report. Do not copy a number from another project.

Then show the funding mix: your own contribution, any loan and any other source. Do not assume a loan will be approved. Our guide on funding a gin brand explains what investors and lenders look for.
Projections and the checks that matter

Present revenue, cost of goods, overheads, interest, tax and profit year by year. Add monthly cash flow for the early period, because that is where small distillers get stuck.

Include these standard tests:

  • Break-even point, in bottles per month.
  • Payback period.
  • NPV and IRR over a stated horizon at a stated discount rate.
  • Sensitivity: sales lower, spirit price higher, a delayed licence.

An illustration with hypothetical numbers: capital of 100 and yearly cash surplus of 25 gives a simple payback of 4 years. Real reports use your own quotations.

List each approval, who grants it and the order in which they come. For India, note that alcohol is a state subject, so the steps and timelines differ between states. Do not quote fees or section numbers. Say that you will confirm the current notification with the regulator or a licensing adviser.

A project report still needs a market section, but keep it modest. Say who you will sell to, in which states or countries and through which channels. Back demand with your own research, such as buyer conversations, shop visits and price checks. See market research before launching a gin.

Avoid market sizes and growth rates you cannot source. A sceptical bank officer will ask where the figure came from. "We visited forty shops and recorded prices" is stronger than a number borrowed from a press release.

Show who is responsible for each stage and when it should finish. A simple schedule covers site and design, equipment order, installation, licences, trial runs and first sale. Be realistic about licences because they depend on the regulator and not on you.

Add the staff you will need: a distiller, a filler or packer, a quality person, a sales lead and an accounts person, even if some roles are shared at first. Show salaries as quoted costs, not guesses.
Reading it as the lender does

Before you submit, read the report as a credit officer would. Do the capital costs match the quotations attached? Does the cash flow include the loan repayment? Does the capacity figure match the still size and the number of shifts? Does the licensing section admit that timing is outside your control?

Inconsistency is the commonest reason a report loses trust. If the equipment list says one still and the revenue assumes two, the reader stops believing the rest. A second person reading it cold, with a red pen, is worth more than another day of polishing.

In project work we often see the same patterns: cost per bottle left out, working capital forgotten, selling prices that ignore what the trade takes and capacity figures that assume perfect running. Fix those four before anything else.

Reports can be prepared remotely. We never promise that a bank will approve a loan.
faqs: Is a DPR the same as a feasibility study?
Close but not identical. A feasibility study asks whether the project should proceed. A DPR assumes it will and details how it will be built and funded.
Someone who understands distilling. A report with a vague process description is easy for a lender to question.
Yes. Costs backed by quotations are far more credible than estimates from memory.
Will a report get my loan approved?
No report can promise that. A clear, consistent report makes it easier for the lender to assess your case.
